dictation.label: Dictation
dictation.summary: SUPER+V, talk, SUPER+V again: what you said is typed into the focused window. A pill at the bottom of the screen shows while it listens.
dictation.size: about 150 MB with the default model

earbuds.label: Earbuds
earbuds.summary: The battery of Nothing earbuds (checked with the Ear (3)): a pill in the bar while they are connected, and a card with left, right and case behind it.

fingerprint.label: Fingerprint
fingerprint.summary: Unlock the lock screen, and sudo in a terminal, with a finger as well as the password. Installs the reader's driver (fprintd, or python-validity for the older Synaptics readers in ThinkPads like the T480), enrols a finger, and adds it to /etc/pam.d/sudo. Installed or not: there is nothing to switch off. Removing it deletes the enrolled fingers and puts sudo back to the password alone.

secureboot.label: Secure Boot
secureboot.summary: Secure Boot with this machine's own keys, and Microsoft's alongside: the firmware boots a signed kernel image (a UKI) directly, and every kernel update is signed as it is built. It stops twice for a step in the BIOS, and carries on when you pick it again. It can't be removed from here: switching it off is a BIOS setting.
secureboot.size: a few MB, and a kernel image on the EFI partition
secureboot.removal: Uninstalling sbctl with Secure Boot on would leave the next kernel update unsigned, and the machine unable to boot. To stop using Secure Boot, switch it off in the BIOS (Security › Secure Boot on a ThinkPad). The kernel image still boots without it, and sbctl can stay.

gpg.label: GPG key
gpg.summary: A quick start: a GPG key of your own (ed25519, with an encryption subkey), in your name and git's email, or asked for when git has none. No passphrase and no expiry, so there is nothing to type or renew. Make a stronger key whenever you like, and put default-key <fingerprint> in ~/.gnupg/gpg.conf so gpg uses it. If you already have a secret key, it is kept and nothing is made. It can't be removed from here: a deleted key can't be brought back.
gpg.removal: Removing the feature would mean deleting your secret key, and whatever it signed or encrypted could no longer be checked or opened. To delete it anyway: gpg --delete-secret-and-public-key <fingerprint>, which gpg --list-secret-keys shows.

weather.label: Weather
weather.summary: The forecast in the bar, and a rail with the week behind it. Needs your coordinates in quickshell/main/.env (see DEPENDENCIES.md).

lazyvim.label: LazyVim
lazyvim.summary: Neovim as LazyVim, cloned fresh from its starter, with this repo's options, keymaps and plugins (nvim/) linked on top. Installed or not: there is nothing to switch off. Removing it deletes ~/.config/nvim and Neovim's data.
lazyvim.size: about 300 MB of plugins, parsers and language servers

ohmyzsh.label: Oh-My-Zsh
ohmyzsh.summary: The zsh framework zsh/.zshrc loads its plugins through (fzf, zoxide, zsh-autosuggestions), cloned fresh from upstream and updating itself. Installed or not: there is nothing to switch off. Without it zsh still starts, with the aliases but none of the plugins.

claudecode.label: Claude Code
claudecode.summary: Anthropic's coding agent in the terminal (claude), from its own installer, and updating itself. Installed or not: there is nothing to switch off. Removing it deletes the program, but not ~/.claude or ~/.claude.json, which hold your login, settings and memory.
claudecode.size: about 230 MB, and it keeps its last few versions

codex.label: Codex
codex.summary: OpenAI's coding agent in the terminal (codex), from its own installer (the one in its GitHub README), which keeps its releases under ~/.codex/packages. Installed or not: there is nothing to switch off. Removing it deletes the program and those releases, but not the rest of ~/.codex, which holds your login and settings.

gemini.label: Gemini CLI
gemini.summary: Google's coding agent in the terminal (gemini), from extra, updated with the rest of the system. Installed or not: there is nothing to switch off. Removing it uninstalls the package, but not ~/.gemini, which holds your login and settings.
gemini.size: about 60 MB, and Node.js if it isn't there yet

opencode.label: OpenCode
opencode.summary: The open-source coding agent in the terminal (opencode), for any model provider, from its own installer into ~/.opencode/bin, which zsh/.zshrc already puts on PATH, and updating itself (opencode upgrade). Installed or not: there is nothing to switch off. Removing it deletes the program and its cache, but not ~/.config/opencode, ~/.local/share/opencode or the plugins in ~/.opencode, which hold your settings and logins.

hermes.label: Hermes
hermes.summary: Nous Research's self-improving agent (hermes), from its own installer, which ends in its setup wizard, and updating itself (hermes update). Installed or not: there is nothing to switch off. Removing it deletes the program, and the Node.js it brought if the system's was too old, but not ~/.hermes itself, which holds your settings, keys, skills and memory.
hermes.size: several hundred MB: its own Python, packages and a browser for its web tools
teardown: for b in node npm npx; do case $(readlink "$HOME/.local/bin/$b") in "$HOME/.hermes/node/"*) rm -f "$HOME/.local/bin/$b" ;; esac; done
